name: Felix Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so please be frank about what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix, 58, and I buy electronic components, chips, connectors, capacitors, for a distributor that sells to repair shops and small manufacturers. I start by asking my AI assistant to summarise overnight price moves and stock shortages, and I read that over a cup of tea. Then I'm on video calls with suppliers in Asia, bidding for stock before someone else grabs it. It's a bit like a trading floor, but quieter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the chase, finding a rare part that's out of stock everywhere and landing it for a small factory that would otherwise shut a line. What wears me out is the time zones, calls at 6 in the morning and 10 at night, and the pace of the market, which has changed three times since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that fits what I see. I use these tools daily and they're good for the routine bits, but they're no magic. At work I'd say, let's use them for what they're good at and spend our own time on the relationships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly comfortable, since my job's solid and I'm already ahead of most buyers on the tools. But I carry a loan, because I co-signed 40,000 for my son's coffee roastery, and it's a worry. If his business wobbled, I'd be the one paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep exploring new tools, and put about 400 a month aside. I'd help my son with his books so he's less likely to wobble, and I'd keep my own credit clean. And I'd keep my evenings free for cycling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels easy, honestly. A small knot about my son's loan, but nothing about AI. I'd say I'm content, with that one worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you co-signed a loan for your son. How would you handle it if his business struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with him and his partner and go through every number, no blame. I could cover three or four months of repayments from my savings, and after that we'd have to make real choices, like selling a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your colleagues about the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them what I do in the morning, the summary of price moves, and say, five minutes and you've done an hour's reading. Some of them look at me like I'm selling something. I'm not, I'm just lazy in a good way.

say: I'd say the tools are **good for routine bits**, so spend our time on relationships.
I'd tell colleagues I use them **daily**.
think: My job is solid and I'm **ahead of most buyers** on the tools.
My worry is the **40,000 loan** I co-signed for my son's coffee roastery.
do: Keep exploring tools and put aside **400 a month**.
Help my son with his **books** so his business is steadier.
Keep my credit **clean** and keep cycling in the evenings.
feel: **Content**, with one small knot about my son's loan.
S0.quote: Five minutes and you've done an hour's reading.
fieldNote: He is the **tool enthusiast** at work and shows colleagues his morning routine.
His unease is **a co-signed loan** for his son's roastery, a household pressure that exists without AI.
Content in outlook, with a practical plan for a shaky month.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for the morning price summary
Carry on buying components and calling suppliers in Asia
Put 400 a month aside as a buffer for the loan
Help my son keep his roastery books in order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I've been waiting for, and it's good, but it's not for everyone. I'd say the buying, the checking and the supplier calls will be done differently. At work I'd say we should make the shift ourselves before it's done to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think there's a gap between me and the rest. I'm ready to be the person who manages the AI doing the buying, but I think half the team is not. A lot of what I do now, such as checking quotes and chasing orders, will be done by the system, and I'll be supervising it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead a pilot where the system handles repeat orders, and I'd review its exceptions. I'd train the team in groups of three on Fridays. I'd also look at my own savings, aiming for an extra two months by next year. And I'd check my son's loan terms so we can refinance if his business needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good and bad. I'm excited, but I know people who won't cope. I'd be uneasy about my son's loan and about what the changes mean for the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd supervise the AI doing the buying. What would you be checking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange orders, like a system buying 10,000 of a chip that's about to be discontinued. Or a supplier that always lies about lead times. The tool is fast but it doesn't know who's honest, and I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beatriz and Hamid, both about 50, who don't use the tools much. They're good at relationships but slow on the screens. I'd offer to sit with them each Friday, because I'd rather lose the argument with a tool than lose a colleague.

say: I'd say this is what I've been **waiting for**, but it's not for everyone.
I'd say we should make the shift before it's **done to us**.
think: I'm ready to **manage the AI** doing the buying, but half the team isn't.
Most of my quote checking and chasing will be done by the **system**.
do: Lead a **pilot** where the system handles repeat orders.
Train the team in groups of three on **Fridays**.
Add **two months** of savings and check my son's loan terms.
feel: Excited, but **uneasy** about colleagues and my son's loan.
S1.quote: The tool is fast but it doesn't know who's honest, and I do.
fieldNote: He sees himself as the **supervisor** of the buying system and not just a user.
The **gap** between him and slower colleagues worries him more than his own job.
His son's loan sits behind every plan, so he builds a **buffer**.

steps.text: Lead a pilot where the system handles repeat orders
Run Friday sessions to train the team in groups of three
Add two months of savings by next year
Check the loan terms so my son's roastery can refinance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is huge, and the world isn't ready. I'd say governments should pay for retraining and a basic income now. I'd tell the team to use the tools hard, because the people who know them will survive longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my desk is gone in about two years. The tools are already doing half of it. I could keep a job supervising the system for a year or two, but eventually it needs fewer of us. With the loan for my son's business and four months of savings, I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on being the one who runs the system, and ask about a role in the firm's AI team. I'd cut my own spending, stop the cycling holidays and put everything toward a cushion. I'd talk to my son about the loan and make a plan. I'd also look at hands-on options through my wife's connections, like a role at the hospital supply office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels intense, like a race. I'd be anxious, but also awake and alert. I'd feel guilty that I'm better prepared than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty about being better prepared. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people around me, Beatriz and Hamid, are no less hard-working than I am. They just didn't use the tools. If I keep my job and they lose theirs, it's partly luck, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's agree now which costs we cut first, and who covers what if sales fall. I'd rather have an awkward talk now than a fight in a year. I'd also tell him not to expand until we know where this goes.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and governments should pay for retraining and basic income.
I'd tell the team to use the tools **hard**.
think: My desk is gone in about **two years**, and the tools already do half of it.
The **loan** and four months of savings make me worried.
do: Go all in on running the system and ask about the firm's **AI team**.
Cut spending and stop the cycling **holidays**.
Make a **plan with my son** about the loan.
feel: **Anxious**, alert and a bit guilty for being better prepared than most.
S2.quote: I'd rather have an awkward talk now than a fight in a year.
fieldNote: Adaptive and fast: his plan is to be the one who **runs the system**.
His **guilt** about colleagues who didn't use the tools is a strong, honest detail.
The family **loan** pulls him from excitement to anxiety.

steps.text: Ask for a role in the firm's AI team
Use the tools hard every day to stay the expert
Stop the cycling holidays and save every spare pound
Agree with my son which costs to cut first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something about it, if we start now. I'd tell the team to start learning and the firm to plan the changes. I'd say publicly that retraining needs to be real, not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's manageable. I'd be 63 by then, which is retirement time anyway, and I'd have time to pay down my son's loan. My bigger worry is for the people who don't see it coming and the market they sell to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the loan faster, get my son's roastery on firmer ground, and keep learning. I'd offer to run training for the team and for local repair shops, maybe as a side business. I'd also plan my retirement: a bike trip, maybe some consulting for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. A touch uneasy, but I feel I'd have it handled. I like having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might run training for local repair shops. Who would pay, and how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shops, or the trade association. A half-day workshop for twenty people, maybe 800. Small shops can't afford consultants, and they'd rather listen to someone who's been buying parts for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you were 45 in this situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go much more cautious, with a mortgage and young kids. At 58 I've got my paid-off years ahead, so I can afford a bit of play. At 45 I'd be worrying about school fees as well.

say: I'd say **five years** is long enough if we start now.
I'd say retraining must be **real**, not a poster.
think: It's manageable, since I'll be **63** by then, around retirement anyway.
I worry for people who **don't see it coming**.
do: Pay down my **son's loan** faster and keep learning.
Offer **training** for the team and for local repair shops.
Plan retirement with **consulting** for small firms.
feel: **Uneasy** but in control, and glad to have time.
S3.quote: Small shops can't afford consultants, and they'd rather listen to someone who's been buying parts for thirty years.
fieldNote: He turns the warning period into a **side business**: workshops for repair shops.
Sees his age as an **advantage**, because he is nearly past the risky years.
Contrast with a 45-year-old shows he is **aware** of his own luck.

steps.text: Pay an extra 500 a month onto my son's loan
Keep learning new tools through the supplier webinars
Run half-day AI workshops for local repair shops
Plan to retire at 63 with some consulting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the people who plan will do well. I'd tell my friends to be curious, not scared. I'd say that firms should invest in their people over this decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. I'd be 68, long retired. I'd be curious to see how the buying world changes, and I'd likely do some advisory work for fun. The only thing I'd watch is my son's business and the state of the market for his generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working normally, keep using the tools, and clear the loan. I'd mentor younger buyers like Priya, and maybe set up a small consultancy at 63. I'd also help my son plan for his business and for the way automation will change his sector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, and kind of hopeful. I'd want to see what happens. I'd feel privileged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mentor younger buyers. What would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read a market, not just the tool. Which suppliers are honest, when to wait, when to grab. It's judgment, and judgment comes from losing money a few times. I'd tell them my losses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your son's business were hurt by automation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help him pivot early, perhaps to selling to businesses rather than people. That's where steady money is. But he's 30 and he'll see it before I do.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and the people who plan will do well.
I'd tell friends to be **curious, not scared**.
think: I'd be fine: **68** and long retired, curious to see how buying changes.
I'd watch **my son's business** and his generation's market.
do: Keep working and using the tools, and clear the **loan**.
S4.quote: Judgment comes from losing money a few times.
fieldNote: Ten years sits beyond his working life, so he feels **calm** and acts as a mentor.
Concerned for **his son**, who is of the exposed generation.
The privilege he mentions again links to his earlier **guilt**.

steps.text: Keep buying and using the AI tools daily
Clear the remaining loan on my son's roastery
Set up a small buying advice consultancy at 63
Help my son plan for automation in his sector

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would hit us before families and firms are ready, and my son's loan would be live. What would help is retraining that exists already, support for people between jobs, and firms being honest about their plans. And a bit of kindness for the people who weren't early on the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm a fan of the tools, but I don't think being a fan makes me smarter than anyone. The people who weren't early are not less deserving. I'd like the world to remember that.

headlineQuote: The people who weren't early are not less deserving. I'd like the world to remember that.

His mood runs from uneasy to **anxious** at two years, and he turns warning time into workshops and consulting.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because it would hit before firms and families are ready and his son's loan would be live.
